questions.q: A die is rolled. Find the probability that an even number is obtained.
questions.explanation: The sample space is $S = \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$. Even numbers are $\{2,4,6\}$, so there are 3 favourable outcomes out of 6 equally likely outcomes.

questions.q: Two coins are tossed. Find the probability that two heads are obtained.
questions.explanation: Sample space: $S = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\}$, so $|S|=4$. Only one outcome gives two heads. Hence $P = \frac{1}{4}$.

questions.q: A die is rolled and a coin is tossed. Find the probability that the die shows an odd number **and** the coin shows a head.
questions.explanation: The two events are independent. $P(\text{odd}) = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$ and $P(H) = \frac{1}{2}$. Therefore $P = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4}$.

questions.q: A card is drawn at random from a deck of cards. Find the probability of getting the **3 of diamonds**.
questions.explanation: There is exactly one 3 of diamonds in a standard 52-card deck.

questions.q: A card is drawn at random from a deck of cards. Find the probability of getting a **queen**.
questions.explanation: There are 4 queens (one per suit) in a standard 52-card deck.

questions.q: A jar contains 3 red marbles, 7 green marbles and 10 white marbles. If a marble is drawn at random, what is the probability that it is **white**?
questions.explanation: Total marbles $= 3 + 7 + 10 = 20$. There are 10 white marbles, so $P = \frac{10}{20} = \frac{1}{2}$.

questions.q:
The blood groups of 200 people are distributed as follows:

| Blood Type | Count |
|---|---|
| A | 50 |
| B | 65 |
| O | 70 |
| AB | 15 |

If a person is selected at random, what is the probability that this person has **O blood type**?
questions.explanation: Out of 200 people, 70 have type O blood. Therefore $P(O) = \frac{70}{200} = \frac{7}{20}$.

questions.q: A die is rolled. Find the probability that the number obtained is **greater than 4**.
questions.explanation: Numbers greater than 4 on a die: $\{5, 6\}$ — 2 favourable outcomes out of 6.

questions.q: Two coins are tossed. Find the probability that **exactly one head** is obtained.
questions.explanation: Sample space: $\{HH, HT, TH, TT\}$. Outcomes with exactly one head: $\{HT, TH\}$ — 2 out of 4.

questions.q: Two dice are rolled. Find the probability that the **sum is equal to 5**.
questions.explanation: Favourable outcomes: $(1,4),\ (2,3),\ (3,2),\ (4,1)$ — 4 pairs. Total outcomes $= 36$.

questions.q: A card is drawn at random from a deck of cards. Find the probability of getting the **King of Hearts**.
questions.explanation: There is exactly one King of Hearts in a standard 52-card deck.

questions.q:
Two dice are rolled. Find the probability that the sum is:

i. Equal to 1
ii. Equal to 4
iii. Less than 13
questions.explanation:
i. The minimum sum with two dice is $1+1=2$, so a sum of 1 is impossible.

ii. Favourable outcomes for sum 4: $(1,3),\ (2,2),\ (3,1)$ — 3 pairs out of 36.

iii. The maximum sum is $6+6=12 < 13$, so this event is certain.

questions.q:
If a die is rolled once, what is the probability that it will show:

i. An even number
ii. An odd number
iii. A prime number
iv. A multiple of 3
v. A multiple of 1
vi. A multiple of 7
questions.explanation:
i. Even: $\{2,4,6\}$ — 3 outcomes.

ii. Odd: $\{1,3,5\}$ — 3 outcomes.

iii. Primes: $\{2,3,5\}$ — 3 outcomes.

iv. Multiples of 3: $\{3,6\}$ — 2 outcomes.

v. Every integer is a multiple of 1, so all 6 faces qualify.

vi. No face value on a standard die is a multiple of 7.
questions.answer:
i. $P(\text{even}) = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

ii. $P(\text{odd}) = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

iii. $P(\text{prime}) = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

iv. $P(\text{multiple of 3}) = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

v. $P(\text{multiple of 1}) = \dfrac{6}{6} = 1$

vi. $P(\text{multiple of 7}) = \dfrac{0}{6} = 0$

questions.q:
If a coin is flipped twice, what is the probability that:

i. It will land heads once and tails once?
ii. It will land heads at least once?
questions.explanation:
Sample space: $\{HH, HT, TH, TT\}$.

i. Favourable outcomes: $\{HT, TH\}$ — 2 out of 4.

ii. Outcomes with at least one head: $\{HH, HT, TH\}$ — 3 out of 4. (Alternatively, $1 - P(TT) = 1 - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}$.)
questions.answer:
i. $P(\text{one head, one tail}) = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

ii. $P(\text{at least one head}) = \dfrac{3}{4}$

questions.q:
A bag contains 4 white counters, 6 black counters, and 1 green counter. What is the probability of drawing:

i. A white counter
ii. A black counter
iii. A green counter
iv. A white counter or a black counter
v. A white counter or a green counter
questions.explanation: Since all events are mutually exclusive, probabilities are added directly where needed.
questions.answer:
Total $= 4 + 6 + 1 = 11$

i. $P(W) = \dfrac{4}{11}$

ii. $P(B) = \dfrac{6}{11}$

iii. $P(G) = \dfrac{1}{11}$

iv. $P(W \cup B) = \dfrac{10}{11}$

v. $P(W \cup G) = \dfrac{5}{11}$

questions.q:
A deck of cards contains 52 cards, 13 from each suit. If a card is flipped over, what is the probability that:

i. It is a spade?
ii. It is a face card (J, Q, K) of any suit?
questions.explanation:
i. There are 13 spades in 52 cards.

ii. There are 3 face cards (J, Q, K) per suit $\times$ 4 suits $= 12$ face cards in total.

questions.q:
Three coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting:

i. All Heads
ii. Exactly one Head
iii. At least one Head
questions.explanation:
Sample space has $2^3 = 8$ outcomes.

i. Only $\{HHH\}$ — 1 outcome.

ii. Outcomes: $\{HTT, THT, TTH\}$ — 3 outcomes.

iii. $1 - P(TTT) = 1 - \frac{1}{8} = \frac{7}{8}$.
questions.answer:
i. $P(HHH) = \dfrac{1}{8}$

ii. $P(\text{exactly one H}) = \dfrac{3}{8}$

iii. $P(\text{at least one H}) = \dfrac{7}{8}$

questions.q:
A box contains 5 red, 3 white and 6 blue balls. If 3 balls are drawn at random, determine the probability that:

i. All 3 are blue
ii. 2 are red and 1 is white
iii. One of each colour is drawn
questions.explanation: The combination formula $\binom{n}{r}$ counts ways to choose $r$ items from $n$ without regard to order.
questions.answer:
Total balls $= 14$, so total ways $= \binom{14}{3} = 364$

i. $P(\text{all blue}) = \dfrac{\binom{6}{3}}{364} = \dfrac{20}{364} = \dfrac{5}{91}$

ii. $P(\text{2 red, 1 white}) = \dfrac{\binom{5}{2}\binom{3}{1}}{364} = \dfrac{10 \times 3}{364} = \dfrac{30}{364} = \dfrac{15}{182}$

iii. $P(\text{one of each}) = \dfrac{\binom{5}{1}\binom{3}{1}\binom{6}{1}}{364} = \dfrac{5 \times 3 \times 6}{364} = \dfrac{90}{364} = \dfrac{45}{182}$

questions.q:
A card is drawn from a well-shuffled pack of playing cards. Find the probability that it is:

i. A club
ii. A king
iii. The ace of spades
questions.explanation: A standard deck has 13 clubs, 4 kings (one per suit), and exactly 1 ace of spades.

questions.q:
Given $P(A) = 0.30,\ P(B) = 0.78,\ P(A \cap B) = 0.16$. Evaluate:

i. $P(A \cup B)$
ii. $P(A^c),\ P(B^c),\ P(A \cup B)^c,\ P(A \cap B)^c$
iii. $P(A^c \cap B),\ P(A \cap B^c),\ P(A^c \cup B),\ P(A \cup B^c)$
iv. $P(A|B),\ P(B|A),\ P(A|B^c),\ P(B|A^c)$
questions.explanation: Use the addition rule $P(A \cup B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B)$, complement rule $P(X^c)=1-P(X)$, and the identities $P(A^c \cap B)=P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ and $P(A^c \cup B)=1-P(A\cap B^c)$.

questions.q:
For two events $A$ and $B$, if $P(A) = 0.2$, $P(B) = 0.3$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.4$. Find:

i. $P(A \cap B)$
ii. $P(A^c),\ P(B^c),\ P(A \cup B)^c,\ P(A \cap B)^c$
iii. $P(A^c \cap B),\ P(A \cap B^c),\ P(A^c \cup B),\ P(A \cup B^c)$
iv. $P(A|B),\ P(B|A),\ P(A|B^c),\ P(B|A^c)$
questions.explanation: Apply the addition rule to find $P(A \cap B)$, then use complement and conditional probability definitions throughout.

questions.q: The probability that a student passes the Statistics course is $\dfrac{2}{3}$, the probability that he passes both Statistics and Mathematics is $\dfrac{14}{45}$, and the probability that he passes at least one course is $\dfrac{14}{15}$. What is the probability that he passes the Mathematics course?
questions.explanation: From the addition rule: $P(S \cup M) = P(S) + P(M) - P(S \cap M)$, rearranging gives $P(M) = P(S \cup M) - P(S) + P(S \cap M)$.

questions.q: A box contains 2 silver and 4 gold coins. A second box contains 4 silver and 3 gold coins. If a coin is selected at random from one box (chosen at random), what is the probability that it is a **gold coin**?
questions.explanation: By the total probability theorem, each box is equally likely to be chosen ($p = \frac{1}{2}$).

questions.q: A problem in statistics is given to 3 students A, B and C whose chances of solving it are $\dfrac{1}{2}$, $\dfrac{3}{4}$ and $\dfrac{1}{4}$ respectively. What is the probability that the problem will be solved?
questions.explanation: Assuming independence, the probability that none of them solves it is the product of their individual failure probabilities.

questions.q: If two dice are thrown, what is the probability that the **sum is equal to 9**?
questions.explanation: Favourable outcomes: $(3,6),\ (4,5),\ (5,4),\ (6,3)$ — 4 pairs out of 36.

questions.q: What is the probability of getting **53 Sundays in a leap year**?
questions.explanation:
A leap year has 366 days $= 52$ complete weeks $+ 2$ extra days. The two extra days can be any consecutive pair:
$$\{\text{Sun–Mon},\ \text{Mon–Tue},\ \text{Tue–Wed},\ \text{Wed–Thu},\ \text{Thu–Fri},\ \text{Fri–Sat},\ \text{Sat–Sun}\}$$
7 equally likely cases. Sunday appears in 2 of them (Sun–Mon and Sat–Sun), so $P = \frac{2}{7}$.

questions.q: Two dice are thrown at random. Let $A$ be the event that the first die shows 2, 5 or 6, and $B$ be the event that the sum of the face values is 9. Check whether $A$ and $B$ are **independent**.
questions.explanation: Two events are independent if and only if $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)$. We verify by listing the favourable outcomes of $A \cap B$: the first die must be in $\{2,5,6\}$ and the sum must be 9. The pairs $(5,4)$ and $(6,3)$ satisfy both conditions, giving $P(A\cap B)=\frac{2}{36}=\frac{1}{18}$.
questions.answer:
$$P(A) = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$$
$$P(B) = \frac{4}{36} = \frac{1}{9} \quad \left[(3,6),(4,5),(5,4),(6,3)\right]$$
$$P(A \cap B) = \frac{2}{36} = \frac{1}{18} \quad \left[(5,4),(6,3)\right]$$

Since $P(A) \cdot P(B) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{1}{18} = P(A \cap B)$,

**$A$ and $B$ are independent.**

questions.q: Sunitha and Saleena stand in a circle with 10 other girls. If the arrangement of 12 girls is at random, find the probability that there are **exactly three girls between Sunitha and Saleena**.
questions.explanation:
Fix Sunitha's position in the circle (removing rotational equivalence). The remaining 11 girls can be placed in $11!$ ways. For exactly 3 girls between Sunitha and Saleena:
- Going clockwise: Saleena is 4 positions away (positions 2,3,4 occupied by 3 girls, Saleena at position 5).
- Going counter-clockwise: Saleena is at position 9 (girls at positions 12,11,10 between them).

So Saleena has 2 valid positions. The remaining 10 girls fill the rest in $10!$ ways.
$$P = \frac{2 \times 10!}{11!} = \frac{2}{11}$$

questions.q: Bag I contains 3 white and 2 black balls. Bag II contains 2 white and 4 black balls. One ball is transferred from Bag I to Bag II, and then a ball is drawn from Bag II. It turns out to be white. What is the probability that the transferred ball was **white**?
questions.explanation:
Define events:
- $W_1$: white ball transferred from Bag I, $P(W_1)=\frac{3}{5}$
- $B_1$: black ball transferred from Bag I, $P(B_1)=\frac{2}{5}$

After transfer, Bag II has 7 balls:
- If $W_1$: Bag II has 3W, 4B $\Rightarrow P(\text{draw W}\mid W_1)=\frac{3}{7}$
- If $B_1$: Bag II has 2W, 5B $\Rightarrow P(\text{draw W}\mid B_1)=\frac{2}{7}$

By total probability:
$$P(\text{draw W}) = \frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{3}{7} + \frac{2}{5}\cdot\frac{2}{7} = \frac{9}{35} + \frac{4}{35} = \frac{13}{35}$$

By Bayes' theorem:
$$P(W_1 \mid \text{draw W}) = \frac{\frac{9}{35}}{\frac{13}{35}} = \frac{9}{13}$$

questions.q: Three firms A, B, and C supply 25%, 35% and 40% of chairs needed by a college. Past experience shows that 5%, 4%, and 2% of the chairs produced by these companies are defective. If a chair is found to be defective, what is the probability that it was supplied by **firm A**?
questions.explanation:
Let $D$ = defective. By total probability:
$$P(D) = 0.25 \times 0.05 + 0.35 \times 0.04 + 0.40 \times 0.02$$
$$= 0.0125 + 0.0140 + 0.0080 = 0.0345$$

By Bayes' theorem:
$$P(A \mid D) = \frac{P(D \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(D)} = \frac{0.25 \times 0.05}{0.0345} = \frac{0.0125}{0.0345} = \frac{25}{69} \approx 0.3623$$

questions.q:
Three urns each contain red and white balls:

| Urn | Red | White |
|---|---|---|
| I | 6 | 4 |
| II | 2 | 6 |
| III | 1 | 2 |

An urn is selected at random and a ball is drawn. If the ball is **red**, what is the probability that it came from **Urn I**?
questions.explanation:
Each urn is selected with probability $\frac{1}{3}$.

$$P(R \mid I) = \frac{6}{10} = \frac{3}{5},\quad P(R \mid II) = \frac{2}{8} = \frac{1}{4},\quad P(R \mid III) = \frac{1}{3}$$

By total probability:
$$P(R) = \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{3}{5} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{71}{60} = \frac{71}{180}$$

By Bayes' theorem:
$$P(I \mid R) = \frac{\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{5}}{\frac{71}{180}} = \frac{\frac{1}{5}}{\frac{71}{180}} = \frac{1}{5}\cdot\frac{180}{71} = \frac{36}{71}$$
